title: Bo (@bo_wangbo) — thread (4 tweets)
summary: [1/4] fyi @olgi In the past years, we've been invested a lot of efforts to build open source softwares, such as Jina/Docarray, and Now we invest more resources on ML as well. ──────── [2/4] Because our belief on open-source, we're planning to release a set of embedding LLMs, contrastively trained on 2B sentence pairs we collected from the internet. The output embeddings can be used for retrieval/measure semantic similarity/sentiment analysis/intent recognition etc ──────── [3/4] We've decided to name it Linnaeus (Linnaeus 3B/7B/15B), after the renowned Swedish botanist, zoologist, and taxonomist, as a way to honor his legacy. While we don't anticipate it to be the top-performing option, we aim to provide an alternative choice beyond API-based calls. ──────── [4/4] We're planning to release 3 embedding LLMs, parameter size will be 3B, 7B and 15B. And freely offer it for anyone for download, modify, research or even use for commercial cases. These models will be EN, later we'll go multilingual.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Oh I want to use it to select hard negatives 😅
Quoting @philipvollet
Our new fusion algorithm: Hybrid search means combining traditional keyword-based and vector searches to get the best of both worlds.
The hard part is combining your different search rankings in the right way. Weaviate steps in and do the hard work for you with our new fusion algorithms.
How does this work
Each of the two (vector and keyword) searches returns a set of results with its own scores.
These scores are then weighted and handed over to the selected fusion algorithm.
A job of the fusion algorithm is to prepare the scores from each search to be compatible with each other, so that they can be added up and presented to the user.
Ranked Fusion
The rankedFusion algorithm is the original hybrid fusion algorithm that has been available since the launch of hybrid search in Weaviate.
In this algorithm, each object is scored according to its position in the results for the given search, starting from the highest score for the top-ranked object and decreasing down the order. The total score is calculated by adding these rank-based scores from the vector and keyword searches.
Relative Score Fusion
In contrast to rankedFusion, however, relativeScoreFusion derives each objects score by normalizing the metrics output by the vector search and keyword search respectively. The highest value becomes 1, the lowest value becomes 0, and others end up in between according to this scale. The total score is thus calculated by a scaled sum of normalized vector similarity and normalized BM25 score.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F4u7ulOaEAAlKk3.png

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
They "test" the vector storage engine Lucence by computing search quality (nDCG@10), which is defined mostly by the model, to then make the claim Lucene is all I need.
With JavaScript and brute force search, I get a higher nDCG@10 score as Lucene. Following the logic in the paper: JavaScript >> Lucene for vector search! I could even use Excel with Visual Basic and get a better vector DB than Lucene (when following the logic in the paper). We all knew that "Excel is All You Need!"
For vector search you are more interested in:
- Latency and queries per seconds at given recall / search quality
- Index size at given recall / search quality
- Index build time
ANN-benchmarks has some good results here, also for Lucene, way more information:
But ANN benchmarks also fall short of a real production test.
A real production test would be like: 1M writes/delete/updates per day for a corpus up to 100M embeddings, 1M queries/day with filters, vertically and horizontally scaled across several machines. How well is Lucene performing here vs. alternatives? How much time is needed to setup and maintain this solution vs alternatives?
You see drastic differences for vector DBs as soon as:
1) You have add/delete/update operations (some can handle it well, other vector DBs deterior in quality & performance)
2) Scaling
3) Robustness & error recovery: How does the cluster react when individual nodes fail?
Lucene doesn't provide 2) and 3) (it is just a framework).
For 1) I think it is not part of Lucence, so you quickly run in scenarios where search quality drops every day (like in the Figure 1, quality starts at 95% recall, then drops after 20 insert/delete cycles to below 90% and gets worse every cycle).
From a vector DB you want 1)+2)+3), Lucene provides none of these.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/F4zrRkuXsAAnfLO.png

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
What can you do if you have $1k in compute credits and a goal?
It turns out quite a lot! I just finished the first version of the paper about NLLB-CLIP - a CLIP model that works in 201 languages! With only 100k samples automatically generated from the @laion_ai COCO dataset, I managed to get SOTA on some benchmarks!
The idea is straightforward - use a pre-trained text encoder from @MetaAI NLLB instead of a standard one. These models have been trained on huge amounts of multilingual data and "understand" all languages very well. That's why we only need to align text and image representations.
And it works! NLLB-CLIP performs comparably with the best models and even beats them for low-resource languages. This is primarily because the training dataset contains all languages equally, which enables good representations in all languages.
One caveat is that you should train only text encoder + projections. As @XiaohuaZhai, @giffmana, @__kolesnikov__, and @_basilM showed in the LiT paper, the image encoder should be frozen to get the best results. I observed the same in my experiments.
Interestingly, this idea doesn't quite work for the largest NLLB encoder - it performs worse than the smaller one. My current hypothesis is that I need more data to fine-tune the encoder this large properly.
Another finding is that the 8-bit Lion optimizer from @Tim_Dettmers's bitsandbytes makes the model converge much faster than AdamW and uses much less memory, which means larger batch sizes!
Many thanks to @boborado and @LambdaAPI for providing compute credits so I could collect the data and run many experiments! I also thank @jasonyo, @savvyRL, and @ml_collective community for the discussions along the way. And special thanks to @AVisheratina for listening my grunts about failing experiments and proofreading the paper =)
Finally, the link to the paper - (yes, I screwed up the paper's title while copying it from LaTeX). I'd appreciate it if you read the paper (it is just 4 pages, workshop-style) and give feedback on improving it or what experiments run next.

some interesting facts about BGE:
1. we thought BGE is bilingual since BAAI released 300 million training data, 100 & 200 million zh & en pairs respectively, while not. bge-en & bge-zh are monolingual models.
2. i am surprised they have a tiny small team, and multi-tasking.
3. not interested in the leaderboard anymore. Too much efforts with little value.
4. hard-negative mining not using bm25 or well-trained dense retrievers, but intermediate checkpoint from pair-wise embedding pre-training.
5. novelty is more important than business value.
6. new technical reports is coming out in January.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Mixtral of Experts by Mistral AI
paper page:
introduce Mixtral 8x7B, a Sparse Mixture of Experts (SMoE) language model. Mixtral has the same architecture as Mistral 7B, with the difference that each layer is composed of 8 feedforward blocks (i.e. experts). For every token, at each layer, a router network selects two experts to process the current state and combine their outputs. Even though each token only sees two experts, the selected experts can be different at each timestep. As a result, each token has access to 47B parameters, but only uses 13B active parameters during inference. Mixtral was trained with a context size of 32k tokens and it outperforms or matches Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5 across all evaluated benchmarks. In particular, Mixtral vastly outperforms Llama 2 70B on mathematics, code generation, and multilingual benchmarks. We also provide a model fine-tuned to follow instructions, Mixtral 8x7B - Instruct, that surpasses GPT-3.5 Turbo, Claude-2.1, Gemini Pro, and Llama 2 70B - chat model on human benchmarks. Both the base and instruct models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GDXoWkBXwAIYirJ.jpg

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo) — thread (3 tweets)
summary: [1/3] We’re finally here with 2 new models, we call it bilingual embedding models, it allows you to perform monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval tasks, the future models are always X+EN, X is the main language and EN as the bridging language. Here are the first two: German-English bilingual embeddings: Chinese-English bilingual embeddings: A Spanish one is coming out very soon, and a technical report is also coming soon on how we enhance model performance on cross-lingual search tasks. You can also use it via api: or Sagemaker: ──────── [2/3] 🇨🇳 jina-embeddings-v2-base-zh 是支持中英双语的文本向量模型，它支持长达8192字符的文本编码。 该模型的研发基于BERT架构(JinaBERT)，JinaBERT是在BERT架构基础上的改进，首次将ALiBi应用到编码器架构中以支持更长的序列。 不同于以往的单语言/多语言向量模型，我们设计双语模型来更好的支持单语言（中搜中）以及跨语言（中搜英）文档检索。 ──────── [3/3] 🇩🇪 jina-embeddings-v2-base-de ist ein zweisprachiges Text Embedding Modell für Deutsch und Englisch, welches Texteingaben mit einer Länge von bis zu 8192 Token unterstützt. Es basiert auf der adaptierten Bert-Modell-Architektur JinaBERT, welche mithilfe einer symmetrische Variante von ALiBi längere Eingabetexte erlaubt. Wir haben, das Model für hohe Performance in einsprachigen und cross-lingual Anwendungen entwickelt und speziell darauf trainiert, gemischte deutsch-englische Eingaben ohne einen Bias zu kodieren.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
It has been shown in various studies that embedding models can perform strong in domain, but have a hard time out-of-domain. Eg in the BEIR paper, DPR was trained on Wikipedia retrieval and is strong there. But on any other dataset it is worse than lexical search.
I also did a quick test for the e5 Mistral model on datasets (robust04, bioasq, signal 1M, TREC news) for which they didn't overfit: Results weren't great, you get the same or better results with 100x smaller (100x cheaper) models.
In-domain performance for embedding models is meaningless if you want to find a good generic Emb model, you always want to evaluate them OOD. By training on all MTEB tasks for these models, the MTEB score for those models become meaningless.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Personally I’m not a big fan of “advanced RAG”, it is so complicated, two or three additional components/logic.
When ppl discussing it, it means current embedding is far from perfect. We will fix them one by one.
Quoting @helloiamleonie
Advanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques address the limitations of naive RAG pipelines.
A recent survey on RAG classifies advanced RAG techniques into pre-retrieval, retrieval, and post-retrieval optimizations.
🔗 Paper:
My latest article gives an overview of advanced RAG techniques:
🦙 Pre-retrieval includes techniques like sliding windows, enhancing data granularity, adding metadata, or optimizing index structures, such as sentence window retrieval.
🦙 Retrieval includes optimizing the embedding models (e.g., fine-tuning) or advanced retrieval techniques like hybrid search
🦙 Post-retrieval includes reranking or prompt compression.
We also implement a naive RAG pipeline using @llama_index and then enhance it to an advanced RAG pipeline using the following:
• Sentence window retrieval (as a pre-retrieval optimization)
• Hybrid search (as a retrieval optimization)
• Re-ranking (as a post-retrieval optimization)

Regards data size, 500-2000 triplets would be more than enough.
The tricky thing is how you define “similar”, your label.

summary:
All of the open embedding models, despite claiming “multilingual”, use extremely skewed language distribution for training (mostly English).
I’m proud of data engineering efforts from our team, managed to harvest ~200 million 🇩🇪 and ~120 million 🇪🇸semantic pairs and triplets to train our bilingual De-En/Es-En embedding model with a beautiful 50:50 ratio.
This leads to a base sized model, beat multilingual-e5-large, match the latest bge-m3 in terms of performance. But 3 times smaller and save 256d per vector.
Quoting @JinaAI_
How did we train DE-EN, ES-EN & ZH-EN bilingual embeddings with 8192-token length? Is a bilingual model superior to a multilingual one? How do they perform on out-of-domain data? Find out in our latest publication. 👇

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Inspired by the LLM lost-in-the-middle paper, @jinaai_ we conducted an interesting experiment to see how long-context encoder was affected by placing correct information at different positions within a long document.
The dataset consists of 2655 Question-Document pairs. Each document contains approximately 4500 words, split into 30 chunks, with each chunk containing about 150 words. Each question has one chunk marked as the "golden match".
The dataset was then replicated 7 times, with the "golden match" inserted at the 0th, 4th, 9th, 14th, 19th, 24th, and 29th positions in each replicate (dot marker). We used jina-v2-small, bge-v1.5-small, and gte-small to encode the question and the long document, and computed cosine similarity, then averaged cosine similarity over the 2655 pairs.
`bge-small`, `gte-small`, `jina-small-1k-chunked`, and `jina-small-2k-chunked` experienced a significant decrease in cos_sim when the "golden match" was placed in the middle or at the end of the document (due to restricted context length).
However, the default `jina-small` with an 8k context length didn’t suffer much. There was only a tiny decrease in average cos_sim, indicating that long context encoder works effectively regardless of the position of the matched information :)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GHlk6HPWsAAq2Le.jpg

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
today i learned something very interesting at ICLR, a term called order of evidence.
During RAG, we send the top retrieved documents as evidences and prompting them to LLMs. Normally prompting is based on cosine similarity: top match always being prompted first.
However, different LLMs might have difference "preference" on the order of evidence:
1. ChatGPT prefers top evidence, which is good.
2. GPT4 has no preference on evidence order, which means the similarity score is not being considered, you only need to decide top-K, and all evidences will be equally treated.
3. Surprisingly, Llama2 and PaLM prefers last order evidence, so you need to reverse the rank list then prompt to the LLM :)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GNJcZRDX0AE7xTU.jpg

there a 2 types of Grounding you can build with @JinaAI_ Reader:
1. you start from a sitemap, convert all urls into LLM friendly plain text, embed into vectors, and when user ask, find the best match and prompt to LLM for generation.
2. Where kicks in: you start with a question, find the up-to-date top-5 information from the web, Reader will turn them into LLM friendly text and prompt to LLM.
Hope you enjoy it (I am, and the team is working on speed improvement)!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GNmqsCLXgAA7xSz.jpg

Grounding is absolutely essential for GenAI applications. Today, we just added new search grounding to the Reader. Now you can simply write a query as 𝗵𝘁𝘁𝗽𝘀://𝘀.𝗷𝗶𝗻𝗮.𝗮𝗶/𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻+𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹+𝘁𝗵𝗲+𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁+𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗫+𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵+𝗯𝗲 and it will return you the top-5 search results from the web, each with LLM-friendly text and a URL pointed to the source. summary:
This notebook is mainly inspired by @bo_wangbo's recent thoughts on using Jina Reader to fetch the full content of a website by following its sitemap.xml for site-level check grounding. This is a super interesting idea, and we'd like to show how to implement it efficiently. We already know that reading a single webpage is super easy, but fetching multiple pages or even an entire site? A simple for-loop is straightforward but not necessarily the most efficient method. What about running a full batch of parallel requests to the Reader API? Well, you'll hit the rate limit in no time.
This notebook serves as a great example, demonstrating how to use Python's asyncio and Semaphore to efficiently query the Reader API without hitting the rate limit. If you haven't used asyncio before, consider this as a good async tutorial.

Proud to be part of this ( I didn’t contribute much).
We started brainstorming a new embedding benchmark at the beginning of the year, focusing on dynamic/ multi domain/ multilingual and RAG friendly. Check it out!
Quoting @JinaAI_
Together with the research team @BAAIBeijing (the creator of bge-m3 embeddings), we are excited to release a new benchmark, AIR-Bench, on @huggingface, focusing on a fair out-of-domain evaluation for RAG & NeuralIR.
AIR-Bench stands for Automated Heterogeneous Information Retrieval Benchmark. It differs from the classic MTEB in three key aspects:
1. It generates synthetic data for benchmarking, ensuring that tests never overlap with training, thus preventing overfitting and data leakage issues common in MTEB and BEIR.
2. It is designed for modern Neural IR, LLM, and RAG pipelines, evaluating not only dense retrievers but also pipelines w/ or w/o rerankers, and it also evaluates the search over very long documents.
3. It can be easily extended to new domains and languages, ensuring the benchmark remains relevant as users' interests continue to expand.
Interested? Read more 👇

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Great work from my colleague @qiliu6777 !
I personally believe the future of embedding model should be focus on recall, and let the LLM judge the final ranking by in context learning. This paper help us validate our hypothesis.
Our JinaCLIP paper also get accepted, see you at @icmlconf .
Quoting @JinaAI_
Can't we just use LLM for reranking? 🤔Just throw the query, doc1, doc2,...docN into the context window and let LLM figure out the top-K? Turns out we can, and it's almost in the way you thought. Announcing our latest research, "Leveraging Passage Embeddings for Efficient Listwise Reranking with Large Language Models," where we introduce PE-Rank, a new LLM-based reranker for efficient listwise passage reranking. Instead of feeding raw text into the LLM context window, we represent each passage using an embedding model as a special token <d1>, <d2>, and then feed the [instruction]+[query]+[special tokens] to the LLM. At inference time, PE-Rank restricts the output space to these special tokens only, enabling more efficient decoding. Overall, PE-Rank greatly reduces the latency from 21s to 3s for reranking 100 documents. But there's more👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GRFP-EjW4AEIAHr.jpg

summary: conduct a very random experiment: TF-IDF weighted mean pooling for text embeddings. Rational: important token should have higher weights than general tokens (even it is already distributed representation). 1. At indexing time, create embeddings together with a tf-idf weight dict. 2. At searching time, multiply tf-idf weights of each token and apply weighted pooling. result: on general dataset, performance is a bit worse than mean pooling. title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
I wrote a blogpost on modality gap for CLIP and JinaCLIP, with additional follow up experiments explaining why it happens:
Quoting @JinaAI_
This is Modality Gap, the reason you can’t just use CLIP models to retrieve texts and images simultaneously and sort the results by score for multimodal retrieval. To understand this better, let’s see how this graph was created: We used the PokémonCards dataset, which contains 13K text-image pairs. These 26K data points were embedded using the Jina-CLIP-v1, and the embeddings were then mapped into 2D space via tSNE. The pairwise relationships are represented by white lines between the cyan and purple dots. Despite enforcing image-text alignment during training, it’s clear that the embeddings don’t form a single, coherent space but instead fall into two distinct subspaces. You can easily draw a boundary between these subspaces, which represents the modality gap between text data and image data.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1828070225771687936/pu/img/0s6j6i7a3muwdXjq.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1828070225771687936/pu/vid/avc1/320x320/zBdz5mo25z6lJn74.mp4?tag=12

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary: spent this summer with my colleague @Robro612 on jina-colbert-v2. at @JinaAI_ If you like ColBERT, and you're working on languages other than English, should give a try (cc @lateinteraction ): 1. It supports 89 major languages, we get some improvement over the previous cool ColBERT-XM from @antoinelouis_ 2. On English we improved compared to jina-colbert-v1 and colbert-2.0, while answerai-colbert-s is too hard to beat 😅 @bclavie 3. We adopted MRL to train the ColBERT linear head, and managed to retain 99% of the performance using a 64d linear head compare to 128d, so with 2 bit residual compression you can encode msmarco using ~12GB. Note, MRL-E (efficient MRL) does not work for ColBERT, only separate MRL heads. Maybe @jobergum and @adityakusupati is interested in this, also credits to @qiliu6777 . 4. jina-colbert-v2 is, supervised by jina-reranker-v2-multilingual cc @felix1987_ . 5. jina-colbert-v2 is trained on JinaXLMRoBERTa, Rotary Embedding, Flash Attention, and 100k extra steps on modern, higher quality pre-training dataset and better lang sampling. summary:
@victorialslocum made a great post on how late chunking works, well explained. 👏
Late-chunking has been integrated into the @JinaAI_ API with a "merge-encode-split" pattern.
Once the API receives a list of texts, it first merges them into a single large document and encodes it into token embeddings using jina-embeddings-v3. The token embeddings are then split according to the original input texts, resulting in chunks of token embeddings corresponding to each text. Finally, mean pooling is applied to each chunk to produce a dense vector.
Quoting @victorialslocum
Optimizing your chunking techniques is one of the top places to improve performance in your RAG pipelines, but what’s the best one?
@JinaAI_ just released a new method called late chunking that takes the same amount of storage space as naive chunking, but solves the problem of lost context similarly to ColBERT.
You can implement it super easily with just a few extra lines in your embedding step!

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
"It's a multilingual embedding model"—okay, but what's that mean? Does it mean you can search German docs with a German query, French docs with a French one, all within the same model? Or can you also search French docs using Japanese queries? A lot of these multilingual models are pretty vague about this: is it just about handling multiple languages separately, or can it do true cross-lingual retrieval? In fact, most models can only manage the former because of the 'language gap'—where similar phrases in different languages don’t align as closely as they should. This makes them less useful for cross-lingual search, which would be much more valuable for global businesses.
While training jina-embeddings-v3, we realized that bridging the language gap isn't straightforward. The two figures below illustrate this. We pre-trained jina-roberta-xlm (the backbone of v3) to see how well it could learn cross-language equivalencies through masked language pre-training. We used UMAP to plot 2D sentence representations for a set of English sentences and their translations into German, Dutch, Simplified Chinese, and Japanese. And it's bad. Comparing this with the final v3 model, it’s clear that the language gap has been significantly reduced. The embeddings in v3 show minimal language-specific clustering, and semantically similar texts produce close embeddings, no matter the language.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
This is a very interesting bug. Let me try to explain how it possibly impacts (@JinaAI_ ) embeddings:
1. We use gradient accumulation to achieve a "pseudo large batch", e.g., 4 (GA steps) * 16 (B) = 64, then perform gradient update. L2 normalization should happen after we reach the "pseudo batch size" (64), while we're actually doing normalization with sub-batch size (16).
2. This means during language model training with the "wrong implementation", using GA will overweight short sequences. The loss on the short sequence length is "scaled up" since their original loss is small, while being normalized by the same value. On the other hand, long sequence length contributions are underestimated.
3. jina-embeddings-v3 training involves 3 steps: masked language modeling -> contrastive training with pairs (InfoNCE with pairs) -> triplet tuning with hard negatives (InfoNCE with hard negatives).
4. During masked language modeling, we continued training XLM-RoBERTa for 160k steps, involving 100k steps with 512 tokens and 60k with variable sequence length up to 8192 tokens, with gradient accumulation steps of 16. So the bug should have a negative impact on stage 1 pretraining.
5. However, to make the training more efficient, we also "group text by similar lengths" (to avoid excessive padding), so the bug's impact was mitigated.
6. During step 2 (contrastive training), to achieve a large batch size, we reduced the max sequence length to 192, so the problem is also minimal.
7. During stage 3, we feed the model with triplets, enlarging sequence length to 512 (or longer) with large gradient accumulation steps (8). This might have a negative impact on the effectiveness of contrastive learning, though how much impact is yet unknown.
Quoting @danielhanchen
Fixed a bug which caused all training losses to diverge for large gradient accumulation sizes.
1. First reported by @bnjmn_marie, GA is supposed to be mathematically equivalent to full batch training, but losses did not match.
2. We reproed the issue, and further investigation showed the L2 Norm betw bsz=16 and ga=16 was 10x larger.
3. The culprit was the cross entropy loss normalizer.
4. We ran training runs with denormalized CE Loss, and all training losses match.
5. We then re-normalized CE Loss with the correct denominator across all gradient accumulation steps, and verified all training loss curves match now.
6. We've already updated @UnslothAI with the fix, and wrote up more details in our blog post here:
This issue impacts all libraries which use GA, and simple averaging of GA does not work for varying sequence lengths.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
very cool idea from @hxiao , you can "see" the semantics by embed the color names:
Quoting @JinaAI_
"Klein blue" is #002FA7, "oak green" is #006F37. What happens if we map those color names into an embedding space and compare it to the real color space? Do they align? Is the embedding space color-continuous? fyi, a color space is a system for organizing colors so devices can accurately reproduce them. Here's what we did: took all 500 color names, embedded them using jina-embeddings-v3, then applied UMAP to reduce to 2D. Visualized via scatterplot, colored data points with their original hex codes. Then added triangulation-based color interpolation for smooth transitions. Here's the result.
This embedding space reveals 2 interesting things: 1) Boundary vertices form clear, smooth color clusters - pure hues dominate the edges. 2) Center mass is a chaotic blend, like a stained glass window in church. Suggests embedding captures 'prototypical' colors distinctly, while mixing gets complex fast. Surprising for jina-v3, trained on general text, not color-specific data. Shows robust capture of color semantics in language. For a general model, it's a quite impressive color manifold.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GaIxbSQbQAA7uiU.jpg

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
JinaCLIP is like CLIP in that it can align text to images, but it's also a text embedding model like jina-embeddings since it's trained to align both text-image and text-text representations.
My colleague @michael_g_u and I did an interesting experiment: what would happen if we just "average" the image and text embeddings from JinaCLIP and used text embedding for search?
Preliminary results:
1. Averaging (or mean pooling) embeddings from two modalities works, and performs better than single modality.
2. Text-to-text search brings higher precision than cross-modal text-image search.
3. Blending two representations into a single dense vector injects visual information and seems to bring more visually diverse results.

curl This is our Meta-Prompt. It allows LLMs to understand our Reader, Embeddings, Reranker, and Classifier APIs for improved codegen. Using the meta-prompt is straightforward. Just copy the prompt into your preferred LLM interface like ChatGPT, Claude, or whatever works for you, add your instructions, and you're set. In this example, we copied the entire prompt into Anthropic Claude and asked it to grab every sentence from Hacker News front page and visualize them using UMAP with matplotlib. This task is nontrivial as it combines multiple APIs from our Search Foundation, like Reader and Embedding where Claude may not have knowledge of. So if you asked Claude directly, it probably wouldn't give an optimal answer. But with the meta-prompt, Claude now has good knowledge about our APIs and can generate much better code! We can copy paste the code directly to Google Colab and with minimum modification, the code just works!

A take with CLIP: global contrastive alignment can incidentally produce a rough local alignment between patches and tokens, but it's an unintended side effect rather than a guaranteed or direct objective of the model. In this example, we take the text tower of jina-clip-v2 and get token-level embeddings of the input sentence, averaging subword embeddings to form "word-level" embeddings. We then compute patch-level embeddings for the input image (each patch is 14x14) and overlay the similarity-based heatmap showing which patches have the highest similarity to that specific word embedding. We run some examples, hoping the visualization can show how the model gets an intuitive sense of "where it might be looking when it sees the word 'Golden.'"

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
The world belongs to agents, but only if they're self-healing.
It's about being resilient in a multi-agent scenario so that the pipeline doesn't break:
AI systems, despite their growing complexity, still break down on the smallest of errors. This halts entire workflows, wastes time, and costs enterprises big.
Now imagine if the same system (all by itself) can detect errors, self-correct, and try again without any human intervention?
This is the promise of Self-healing Agents!
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐟-𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠
The self-healing aspect of an agent refers to its ability to detect errors or inconsistencies in its output and automatically retry with adjusted parameters or prompts via a corrective feedback loop.
How it all works:
• First Attempt: The agent attempts to perform its task normally and produces an output.
• Validation: A validation test checks the agent's output for accuracy.
• Error Detection: If an error is detected, a self-healing (corrective) loop is triggered.
• Feedback: Error details are sent back to the agent. The agent reflects on its previous approach, refines its prompts, or even requests additional information.
• Retry: The agent reattempts the task, using the insights from the corrective loop.
This cycle repeats until the validation test is satisfied with the generated output or a predetermined timeout (max number of retries) is reached.
𝐃𝐀𝐆 → 𝐄𝐃𝐀
To build self-healing agents, there needs to be a shift from graph-based architecture to event-driven architecture (EDA). Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) have limitations when it comes to building agentic systems that can self-heal as they lack loops.
Event-driven Architecture (EDA) on the other hand, supports loops through event-based communication, allowing components to interact repeatedly by triggering specific events. EDA also supports the use of ‘states’ that enables data sharing and propagation, which improves communication and coordination between different components.
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐬?
Increased reliability, reduced downtime, less manual intervention, and most importantly better UX!
As we move forward to a time where AI systems are expected to be mission-critical, self-healing capabilities (powered by corrective feedback loops) will become increasingly essential to empower reliable and trustworthy AI-powered solutions!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GhAYHQcWAAAZOyA.jpg

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary: I read the Gemini embedding paper. Despite not being short, it reveals not much information. 1. Performance seems very good, evaluated at 3072d—2-3 times larger than a typical model—and supports MRL. 2. The backbone model size is unknown. They turned a decoder-only model into a bidirectionally trained one with mean pooling. Considering Gemma is a smaller version of Gemini, it could exceed 27B. 3. Mentions that pair training (Q, Pos) + large batch size helps, though previous research suggested this is less effective for decoder-only models. 4. Uses Gemini for data filtering and proves it works well. We observed something similar at @JinaAI_ . 5. Applies model soup/weight merging—we did the same for Jina-embeddings-v3/reader-lm-v2. 6. No black magic, everything seems to be quite "common", big model, better data, big compute, better result. 7. Has 48 authors 😅.

summary: TL;DR: How Embedding/Reranker/Reader are becoming crucial components in serving 1. title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
DeepSeek takes the lead: DeepSeek V3-0324 is now the highest scoring non-reasoning model
This is the first time an open weights model is the leading non-reasoning model, a milestone for open source.
DeepSeek V3-0324 has jumped forward 7 points in Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, now sitting ahead of all other non-reasoning models. It sits behind DeepSeek’s own R1 in Intelligence Index, as well as other reasoning models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Alibaba, but this does not take away from the impressiveness of this accomplishment. Non-reasoning models answer immediately without taking time to ‘think’, making them useful in latency-sensitive use cases.
Three months ago, DeepSeek released V3 and we we wrote that there is a new leader in open source AI - noting that V3 came close to leading proprietary models from Anthropic and Google but did not surpass them.
Today, DeepSeek are not just releasing the best open source model - DeepSeek are now driving the frontier of non-reasoning open weights models, eclipsing all proprietary non-reasoning models, including Gemini 2.0 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Llama 3.3 70B. This release is arguably even more impressive than R1 - and potentially indicates that R2 is going to be another significant leap forward.
Most other details are identical to the December 2024 version of DeepSeek V3, including:
➤ Context window: 128k (limited to 64k on DeepSeek’s first-party API)
➤ Total parameters: 671B (requires >700GB of GPU memory to run in native FP8 precision - still not something you can run at home!)
➤ Active parameters: 37B
➤ Native FP8 precision
➤Text only - no multimodal inputs or outputs
➤ MIT License

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
Yesterday's bagging & boosting; today's model soups. It involves training multiple models with different hyperparameters or data partitions — the same as you usually would — but then combining them. The result is a better and more robust model than the single best performer. At Jina, we used this technique to train our jina-embeddings-v3 and ReaderLM-v2. For example, multilingual embedding models often suffer from biases and performance failures caused by inbalanced training data. It would be a boon to be able to train the best model we can on each task or dataset individually and then combine them equally.

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
I was lucky to work in both China and the US LLM labs, and I've been thinking this for a while. The current values of pretraining are indeed different:
US labs be like:
- lots of GPUs and much larger flops run
- Treating stabilities more seriously, and could not tolerate spikes in large flops run, thus invented so many stability-related tricks, including all kinds of soft-cap, MuP, and spectral norm control tricks
- Treats predictabilities more seriously. Check GPT 4 report for reference, even trying to predict the eval task performances
- Because of the stability and predictability ask, treats hyper-params and optimization more seriously
- Generally believe more in data, optimization than arch
China labs be like:
- has very limited GPUs, e.g. k2 in 4k GPU and v3 in 2k GPU
- as a result, pushing for the limit of pretrain modeling-infra co-design, see so many tricks in V3, and K2 has some cool stuff too (the offload trick helps remove the stupid MoE gating constrain and only uses EP 16)
- cares model arch/token efficiency over optimization, stability
- cares more about data quality than data quantity
- taking inference into consideration day 0, even before the training starts
In general, China labs are trying to use <4e+24 flops models to catch up with >1e+25 flops models. It is hard or impossible, but they are making good progress.
I am actually very happy to see Qwen's new try on model archs, they used to be focusing more on data side rather than on model arch side. They developed linear attn, not just for people to think they are innovating, it is actually considering pushing the limit for test time scaling. Llama4 failed for many reasons, but qwen-next is different. They just used very limited flops and it is a brave try for good reasons.
Quoting @CharuruCha14310
@teortaxesTex @JingyuanLiu123 I bet OpenAI/xAI is laughing so hard, this result is obvious tbh, they took a permanent architectural debuff in order to save on compute costs.

summary:
Tool Search Tools, but text embeddings as the retriever:
Following the Anthropic blog, I manually crafted this MTEB format benchmark and collected 580 real-world tools from 20 sites, generated synthetic query/prompt per tool and compared a set of models:
1. BM25 again, a strong baseline, .7 Recall@3.
2. Later/SOTA embedding models does not necessarily perform significantly better. all-minilm-l6-v2 despite only have 30m parameters, got .8 Recall@3.
3. Fine-tuning works, ToolRet (bge-finetune) give a boost on Recall@1, .9 Recall@3.
4. When Query is hard to grep, embedding seems to be the best approach.
5. Everything is OOD, without seen any benchmark data.

Most people know Perplexity for Sonar. This is Sonar on steroids.
Quoting @perplexitydevs
Perplexity's Agent API presets have been refreshed: faster, smarter, cheaper while maintaining full computer and usage transparency.
Most agentic API endpoints charge a fixed per-request rate in the name of simplicity.

On Agent API, it's simple and transparent:
> Pick preset mode: fast / low / medium / high depending on task complexity
> Pay only for the inference and tools you actually use (direct model provider pricing)

summary:

title: Bo (@bo_wangbo)
summary:
🫡🫡🫡
Quoting @ArtificialAnlys
Perplexity Search debuts on the Artificial Analysis Search Index, with all three context size variants taking top positions on the leaderboard
The @perplexity_ai Search API comes with three context settings (low, medium, and high) that control how much extracted content each search result carries. We tested all three variants using our standardized methodology: the same model (GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning), running inside Stirrup, our open-source agent harness, with tools for searching and fetching pages from the web. Only the provider behind the search tool changes.
Key results:
➤ Perplexity Search (medium) scores 80 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index, ahead of the previous leaders, Parallel (advanced) and Brave Search (LLM context), at 75. The high and low variants score 79 and 77 respectively. Its lead is concentrated in BrowseComp results, with AA-Omniscience and DeepSearchQA scoring comparably to other leading providers
➤ Efficient search payloads: smaller overall search results mean the model reads less per task, so Perplexity has the lowest model inference cost per task of providers we’ve tested so far, ranging from $0.028 to $0.034 across the three variants vs $0.036 for the next lowest provider
➤ Total cost per task is ~$0.091 for the medium and high context variants, at mid-pack latency. For comparison, Parallel (advanced) costs $0.084 per task and Brave (LLM context) costs $0.13 per task
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQ1ZnNMWwAA0omb.jpg
